name: Why a step was done
sub: The purpose of a part of the procedure
rule: Every step in an experiment has a reason: to keep something constant, to measure something, or to make sure the result is real. The reason is usually the thing that would go wrong if you skipped the step.
trick: Ask "what if they hadn't?" Whatever would have gone wrong is why the step was there.
passage: Students measured how fast ice melts in different liquids. Before each trial, they let every liquid sit in the room for an hour. Then they added one ice cube of the same size to each cup and timed how long it took to melt.

examples.text: Why let the liquids sit for an hour? So they all start at the same temperature.
examples.note: What if they hadn't? A warm liquid would melt ice faster for the wrong reason.

examples.text: To make the experiment take longer.
examples.note: Nothing in science is done for its own sake.

another.text: Imagine a race where one kid gets a head start. Not fair, right? Scientists do steps like "same-size cups" and "same temperature" so the race is fair. When a question asks why a step was done, the answer is usually "to make it fair" or "to measure something."
another.example:
Same-size ice cubes → fair race
Same starting temperature → fair race
A thermometer in each cup → to measure

questions.passage: A student tested which paper towel absorbs the most water. She cut every towel to the same size, dipped each one for exactly 10 seconds, and then weighed it.
questions.stem: Why did she cut every towel to the same size?
options: So that a bigger towel couldn't absorb more just by being bigger
To make them fit in the water
Because the scale was small
questions.why: What if she hadn't? The biggest towel would win no matter what it's made of. Same size makes it fair.

questions.passage: A chemist repeated each measurement three times and reported the average.
options: To use up the chemicals
To make the number look bigger
To reduce the effect of a single odd measurement
questions.why: One reading can be off. Three readings averaged smooth out a mistake or a fluke.

name: Designing the next experiment
sub: Change one thing to answer a new question
rule: To answer a new question, change the one variable the question is about and keep everything else exactly as before.
trick: Find the new question's key word. The next experiment changes that one thing. If the question is about temperature, vary temperature and nothing else.
passage: Study 1 tested how the amount of salt affects how fast water boils. All trials used 1 liter of water on the same burner.

examples.text: New question: does the amount of water matter? Next step: same burner, same salt, vary the liters.
Vary the water amount and the burner.
examples.note: Two changes. You couldn't tell which one caused the difference.

another.text: You have three light switches and don't know which one runs the kitchen light. Flip one at a time. If you flip two at once and the light comes on, you still don't know which switch did it. Experiments change one thing at a time for the same reason.
another.example:
Flip A → light on → A does it
Flip A and B → light on → could be either

questions.passage: Experiment 1 measured how far a toy car rolls off ramps of different heights. Every ramp was 1 meter long and covered in the same smooth plastic.
questions.stem: To find out whether the ramp surface affects distance, the next experiment should:
options: Use one ramp height and try several surfaces
Try several heights with a carpet ramp
Use a longer ramp
questions.why: The new question is about surface, so vary surface. Keep height fixed so it can't be the cause.

questions.passage: A trial found that a plant food increased tomato yield in sandy soil.
questions.stem: To learn whether it also works in clay soil, researchers should:
options: Test a different plant food in clay soil
Repeat the same trial with the same plant food in clay soil
Add more plant food to the sandy soil
questions.why: Keep the plant food, change the soil. Changing the food too would mix up two questions.

name: Does the data support it?
sub: Checking a claim against the numbers
rule: A claim is supported only if the numbers actually move the way the claim says. Check the table before you agree with anything.
trick: Turn the claim into a prediction about the table ("if this is true, column B should go up"). Then look. Does it?

examples.text: Claim: more fertilizer helps up to a point. Supported.
examples.note: Height rises to 10 g, then flattens. The table shows exactly that.

examples.text: Claim: more fertilizer always helps. Not supported.
examples.note: 15 g gave the same height as 10 g.

another.text: Someone says "I always win at checkers." You look at the scoreboard: they lost once. "Always" is broken. Check every row of the table against the claim. Words like always, never, and doubles are easy to break with just one row.
another.example:
Claim: the plant doubled every week.
Table: 10, 20, 35
35 is not double 20. Not supported.

questions.stem: Claim: Going from 10 g to 15 g of fertilizer made plants taller. Is it supported?
options: Yes
No, height was 21 cm at both amounts
questions.why: Same height in both rows. The extra 5 g did nothing.

questions.stem: Which claim does the table best support?
options: Fertilizer has no effect on height.
Height increases with fertilizer up to about 10 g, then levels off.
Height doubles for every 5 g added.
questions.why: Up, up, flat. That is the only claim that fits every row.

name: Two scientists disagree
sub: Finding what each one actually claims
rule: When two scientists disagree, each one has a main claim and reasons for it. Pin down each claim in one sentence before answering anything about them.
trick: Write "Scientist 1 says ___ because ___. Scientist 2 says ___ because ___." Most questions are answered by those two lines.
passage:
Scientist 1: The lake's fish are dying because fertilizer from nearby farms runs into the water and feeds algae, which uses up the oxygen.

Scientist 2: The fish are dying because the summers have grown hotter, and warm water holds less oxygen.

examples.text: They agree fish are dying from low oxygen. They disagree on what caused it.
Scientist 2 thinks the fish are fine.
examples.note: Both accept the fish are dying.

another.text: Two kids find a broken vase. Both agree the vase is broken and the cat was in the room. Kid 1 says the cat did it. Kid 2 says the wind did it. They agree on what happened. They fight about why. Find the one word where the "why" splits.
another.example:
Both agree: fish are dying, oxygen is low
Split: farm runoff vs hot summers

questions.passage:
Scientist 1: The lake's fish are dying because fertilizer runs into the water and feeds algae, which uses up the oxygen.

Scientist 2: The fish are dying because summers are hotter, and warm water holds less oxygen.
questions.stem: On what do both scientists agree?
options: Farms are to blame.
The fish are dying from low oxygen.
Summers are hotter.
questions.why: Both say fish are dying and both say oxygen is low. They split only on the cause.

questions.passage:
Scientist 1: The lake's fish are dying because fertilizer runs into the water and feeds algae, which uses up the oxygen.

Scientist 2: The fish are dying because summers are hotter, and warm water holds less oxygen.
questions.stem: Which finding would support Scientist 1 over Scientist 2?
options: Fish deaths are highest right after heavy rain washes fields into the lake.
Fish deaths are highest in the hottest weeks.
Fish deaths happen all year equally.
questions.why: Rain carrying fertilizer in points to the farm explanation. Hot weeks would support Scientist 2.

name: Picking the better explanation
sub: Which idea fits all the data
rule: The better explanation is the one that fits every observation, not just most of them. One observation that an explanation can't handle is a serious problem for it.
trick: Test each explanation against each row of data. The first one to hit a row it can't explain loses.

examples.text: Explanation: flooding happens when drains aren't cleaned. Fits every row.
examples.note: Every "No" clean is a flood, every "Yes" clean is dry.

examples.text: Explanation: flooding happens when it rains a lot. Fails.
examples.note: May flooded with 2 inches; June stayed dry with 7.

another.text: A good explanation is like a weather friend who's always right. Ask each explanation to guess every day on the list. The one that's never wrong wins. Being right most days isn't good enough when the other one is right every day.
another.example:
Explanation A: wrong on 2 days out of 4
Explanation B: right on all 4 → B is better

questions.stem: Which explanation fits all four months?
options: Flooding depends on how much rain falls.
Flooding happens when the drains were not cleaned.
Flooding happens in spring only.
questions.why: Check each row: uncleaned drains always flood, cleaned drains never do. Rainfall fails in May and June.

questions.stem: Which month is the biggest problem for the rainfall explanation?
options: March
April
June
questions.why: 7 inches, the most rain of any month, and no flooding. The rainfall model can't explain that.
